DEAR ABBY: I was in a relationship with a married man for more than 20 years. A year ago, I found out he was cheating on me, so I ended the relationship. We have four children under the age of 18, and our relationship has caused them nothing but heartache because he chose his wife over them.

I was so blinded by having the family I yearned for that I didn’t see how toxic the relationship was to everyone. I’m working toward building a better relationship with my children, but I think it’s hard for them to trust me because of my previous refusal to end my involvement with him. Do you have any suggestions besides time to bring us closer? — BLINDED BY HIM IN THE NORTH

DEAR BLINDED: Did you really tell your children that your lover had chosen his wife over them? If you did, it was heartless. They had nothing to do with his unwillingness to commit to you, and for the sake of their self-esteem you should make that clear.

Family counseling might help bring you closer to your children. It may also help you come to terms with the fact that you wasted so many years on this man — and understand why you did it — so you can move on. If you can manage that, there’s hope that they can, too.

DEAR ABBY: We recently did a favor for a young couple who work for us. We were happy to do it and did not expect or want any type of repayment. They decided to thank us with a nice gift of tickets to an event that takes place on a day when we are unavailable. In addition, it is three hours away from us, and, due to my mobility issues, we cannot take a long trip in the car. It’s also not something we would normally be interested in.

It seems strange and random that someone would give us such a gift, not knowing if we’re available, interested or able. I graciously thanked them for the gift and told them that we’re not going to be able to use it and why. I suggested that they try to give it to somebody else who can use the tickets. They were not cheap! I’m feeling bad now for rejecting the gift. But if we had accepted it and pretended we were going to like and use it, it would have been a lie. Did I do the right thing? — RETHINKING REJECTION

DEAR RETHINKING: When you receive a material gift in a reasonable price range, it’s usually best to accept it politely and not explain why you can’t or won’t use it. However, because these were pricey tickets to an event, and accepting would have deprived someone else of the ability to attend, you did exactly the right thing. The key is to be prompt and polite in your refusal, which you were. Imagine the awkwardness if you had lied and they later asked whether you had enjoyed yourselves at the event!

news.originalTitle: How women scavenge scraps from lithium to earn a living in Nigeria
news.title: How women scavenge scraps from lithium to earn a living in Nigeria
news.originalSummary:
How women scavenge scraps from lithium to earn a living in Nigeria

Dozens of women sift through the waste left behind by lithium miners in Nigeria, digging for traces of ore to resell. Nigeria’s lithium industry is estimated to be worth over $34bn, but these workers only take home about $15 a week. In collaboration with Light Oriye Tamunotonye.

news.originalContent:
The IRGC says the attack is part of efforts to counter ‘hostile activities of US forces in the region’.

A drone attack has been thwarted in Bahrain, according to the Gulf country’s state television, after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched the barrage.

The IRGC said on Tuesday that it carried out a drone attack on a US radar system at the Isa airbase in Bahrain.

The reported attacks in Bahrain – which is home to the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet – come amid stalled diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war ⁠on Iran, which began ⁠on February 28 and has spread across the region.

It is the latest of several Iran-claimed attacks on US radar systems in the Gulf country in recent days.

The IRGC said the attack was “part of efforts to counter the hostile activities of US forces in the region”, according to a statement carried by Iran’s IRIB broadcaster.

Blasts echoed over the Bahraini capital Manama after residents received a mobile phone alert warning of a “potential threat”. Explosions were heard after the Interior Ministry’s alert urged residents to “proceed to the nearest safe location”.

On Sunday, the IRGC launched six drones at a US air defence radar system at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base, which hosts US forces, in response to what it described as hostile US actions.

On Friday, the IRGC also claimed to have targeted a US early-warning radar facility in Bahrain, but the US military denied that the facility had been hit, saying it intercepted two Iranian drones without damage or injuries.

Bahrain has faced renewed security concerns amid escalating tensions between Washington and Tehran.

This is a developing news story…

news.originalContent:
Ronaldo’s mother Dolores Aveiro said she was glad to see Jesus suffer his first defeat after her son had been ‘deceived’ by him.

Portugal coach Jorge Jesus believes he will still be responding to questions about Cristiano Ronaldo next year, after he was asked for his thoughts on scathing comments by the football great’s mother.

“Now I have to respond to Cristiano Ronaldo’s mother?” Jesus asked on Tuesday, addressing the media before Portugal’s final Nations League group fixture away to Wales.

“I don’t know when it is going to stop. If you guys ask the questions, I have to answer. If you ask about Ronaldo next year, I will answer.”

Jesus’s frustration stemmed from his lingering tensions with Ronaldo following the recent international retirement of football’s all-time greats.

The 72-year-old head coach responded to comments from Ronaldo’s mother in the wake of the team’s latest defeat – their first since the 41-year-old forward quit national duties.

Jesus wondered when he would stop being peppered about Ronaldo after a 4-1 Nations League defeat to Denmark prompted criticism from the five-time Ballon d’Or winner’s mother, Dolores Aveiro.

Aveiro said she was glad to see Jesus suffer his first defeat since taking charge after the World Cup as Ronaldo had been “deceived” by the former Benfica boss.

Ronaldo’s decision to hang up his boots for country followed a falling out with Jesus, who was previously the superstar’s coach at Saudi club Al-Nassr.

The ex-Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus star accused Jesus of broken promises after he was asked to warm up during a match against Norway in September without being introduced as a substitute.

Ronaldo left the team camp and was handed a 30-day suspension and a token fine.

He apologised and was expected to return to the Portugal squad, but instead brought down the curtain on a 23-year international career.

His 234 appearances and 146 goals are both world records in the men’s game.

Ronaldo’s lack of mobility was often pinpointed as a factor in a richly talented Portugal squad falling short in recent major tournaments.

Jesus’s side had made a perfect start with four consecutive wins prior to Saturday’s shock defeat to the Danes.

“After the game against Denmark, everyone is asking me about different individuals, not about the team or winning here,” added Jesus.

“We played one bad game and it’s harder to move on when we have a result like that, but we are going to try and win the game.”

Portugal only need a point in Cardiff to secure top spot in Nations League group A4 against a Wales side that will finish bottom of the section.

“You were all having a go at him for playing, and then as soon as he retires, suddenly it’s all hell breaking loose!” Wales boss Craig Bellamy told the Portuguese media.

“He is one of the best players that has ever played the game. We’re all going to miss him.”

news.originalContent:

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani drew widespread criticism on Monday after he announced that he would dissolve the specialized New York City Police Department counterterror unit, which also manages crowds during protests, and replace it with a civilian-led “community dialogue and de-escalation division” and a “First Amendment support team.”

City Hall called the de-escalation division a “first-of-its-kind” and said that it “will not have weapons or arrest powers.”

“During our campaign, I promised New Yorkers that we would disband the Strategic Response Group and separate counterterrorism from protest response, and today we are delivering on that promise,” Mamdani said.

“New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat,” he said. “We are establishing a new, civilian-led approach that prioritizes dialogue, engagement and de-escalation.”

The NYPD Strategic Response Group was formed in 2015.

Police officers can still be “called upon to come make arrests, including for those engaging in civil disobedience,” Mamdani said.

The new civilian-led unit will “not have weapons or arrest powers,” and the NYPD support team “will consist of 30 uniformed officers trained in communication and de-escalation,” according to City Hall.

It added that police won’t be allowed to use tear gas or pepper spray during “First Amendment activities,” and that “kettling,” a crowd-control tactic in which officers confine protesters to a restricted space, will end.

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said that she “would never support changes that diminish the NYPD’s ability to protect New Yorkers or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat.”

“These changes will make us a stronger, more effective department,” she said.

Inna Vernikov, a member of the New York City Council and co-chair of its bipartisan task force on Jew-hatred, told JNS that “by disbanding the SRG, Mamdani is also unleashing a monster on Jewish New Yorkers.”

“Our community has already endured violent protesters attacking Jewish-owned businesses, intimidating congregants at synagogues and threatening Jewish students on university campuses,” she said. “Apparently, that’s not enough.”

“What’s another target painted on the backs of New York’s Jews for this mayor?” Vernikov told JNS.

Evan R. Bernstein, CEO of B’nai B’rith International, told JNS that the mayor’s decision is “a dangerous and ideological betrayal of public safety, especially for New York’s Jewish community.”

“At a moment when Jews remain the city’s most targeted group for hate crimes, the SRG has been one of the few specialized units capable of rapidly containing violent, antisemitic protests that have repeatedly targeted synagogues, Jewish institutions and ordinary New Yorkers,” he said.

“Replacing trained officers with an unarmed, civilian ‘dialogue’ division that has no arrest powers is not reform. It is willful blindness,” Bernstein said. “Dialogue does not stop mobs chanting for intifada or blocking streets outside of Jewish neighborhoods.”

Mamdani’s decision follows calls from anti-Israel groups, which have staged protests outside synagogues and Jewish institutions across the Big Apple, to nix the NYPD unit.

In May, an anti-Israel protest outside a Brooklyn synagogue led to multiple arrests, and an NYPD officer was hospitalized after anti-Israel protesters tried to remove barriers outside Park East Synagogue in Manhattan.

The city recorded an 182% increase in anti-Jewish hate crimes in January, in Mamdani’s first month as mayor, and since then, more than half of the city’s hate crimes have targeted Jews, who make up about 10% of New Yorkers.

Last month, 57.8% of hate crimes in New York City targeted Jews, according to city data. Jewish leaders in the city and nationwide have told JNS that the mayor’s rhetoric, including his frequent and widespread criticism of Israel, has made Jews less safe.

Chaim Steinmetz, senior rabbi of Congregation Kehilath Jeshurun, a Modern Orthodox synagogue on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, told JNS that the mayor’s decision will have a negative impact on Jews.

“At issue is not protest as free speech. That must be sacrosanct,” the rabbi said. “What is of deep concern to the Jewish community is protest as intimidation.”

At recent demonstrations outside the UJA building and Park East Synagogue, protesters intimidated Jews, according to Steinmetz.

“Zohran Mamdani is acting like the protester-in-chief, not the mayor of New York,” he told JNS. “Because of that, there will be many more events like Park East Synagogue.”

“When there is violence,” he said, “it will be Mamdani’s fault.”

The World Jewish Congress told JNS that it has “every confidence” in the NYPD’s ability to protect Jews despite the changes.

“Politics must never get in the way of protecting Jewish lives,” it said.

Moshe Davis, former executive director of the mayor’s office to combat Jew-hatred under Mayor Eric Adams, told JNS that “we need more cops and faster responses when mobs target our community.”

“I hope this fancy video and rebrand won’t change that,” Davis, who leads the Protecting Worship coalition, told JNS. “If the mayor’s new de-escalation unit can convince his own allies to stop targeting houses of worship, we’ll all welcome it.”

Jim Geraghty, senior political correspondent at National Review, addressed the Mamdani decision on his podcast “Three Martini Lunch.”

“You’ve basically announced this is your permission slip,” he said. “This doesn’t work in other cities. Why it would work in New York is completely beyond me, but it feels very on brand for Mamdani to say, ‘I’m going to do everything I can to make my city feel more chaotic and more like an angry mob is really in control.’”

It added that police won’t be allowed to use tear gas or pepper spray during “First Amendment activities,” and that “kettling,” a crowd-control tactic in which officers confine protesters to a restricted space, will end.

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said that she “would never support changes that diminish the NYPD’s ability to protect New Yorkers or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat.”

“These changes will make us a stronger, more effective department,” she said.

Inna Vernikov, a member of the New York City Council and co-chair of its bipartisan task force on Jew-hatred, told JNS that “by disbanding the SRG, Mamdani is also unleashing a monster on Jewish New Yorkers.”

“Our community has already endured violent protesters attacking Jewish-owned businesses, intimidating congregants at synagogues and threatening Jewish students on university campuses,” she said. “Apparently, that’s not enough.”

“What’s another target painted on the backs of New York’s Jews for this mayor?” Vernikov told JNS.

Evan R. Bernstein, CEO of B’nai B’rith International, told JNS that the mayor’s decision is “a dangerous and ideological betrayal of public safety, especially for New York’s Jewish community.”

“At a moment when Jews remain the city’s most targeted group for hate crimes, the SRG has been one of the few specialized units capable of rapidly containing violent, antisemitic protests that have repeatedly targeted synagogues, Jewish institutions and ordinary New Yorkers,” he said.

“Replacing trained officers with an unarmed, civilian ‘dialogue’ division that has no arrest powers is not reform. It is willful blindness,” Bernstein said. “Dialogue does not stop mobs chanting for intifada or blocking streets outside of Jewish neighborhoods.”

Mamdani’s decision follows calls from anti-Israel groups, which have staged protests outside synagogues and Jewish institutions across the Big Apple, to nix the NYPD unit.

In May, an anti-Israel protest outside a Brooklyn synagogue led to multiple arrests, and an NYPD officer was hospitalized after anti-Israel protesters tried to remove barriers outside Park East Synagogue in Manhattan.

The city recorded an 182% increase in anti-Jewish hate crimes in January, in Mamdani’s first month as mayor, and since then, more than half of the city’s hate crimes have targeted Jews, who make up about 10% of New Yorkers.

Last month, 57.8% of hate crimes in New York City targeted Jews, according to city data. Jewish leaders in the city and nationwide have told JNS that the mayor’s rhetoric, including his frequent and widespread criticism of Israel, has made Jews less safe.

Chaim Steinmetz, senior rabbi of Congregation Kehilath Jeshurun, a Modern Orthodox synagogue on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, told JNS that the mayor’s decision will have a negative impact on Jews.

“At issue is not protest as free speech. That must be sacrosanct,” the rabbi said. “What is of deep concern to the Jewish community is protest as intimidation.”

At recent demonstrations outside the UJA building and Park East Synagogue, protesters intimidated Jews, according to Steinmetz.

“Zohran Mamdani is acting like the protester-in-chief, not the mayor of New York,” he told JNS. “Because of that, there will be many more events like Park East Synagogue.”

“When there is violence,” he said, “it will be Mamdani’s fault.”

The World Jewish Congress told JNS that it has “every confidence” in the NYPD’s ability to protect Jews despite the changes.

“Politics must never get in the way of protecting Jewish lives,” it said.

Moshe Davis, former executive director of the mayor’s office to combat Jew-hatred under Mayor Eric Adams, told JNS that “we need more cops and faster responses when mobs target our community.”

“I hope this fancy video and rebrand won’t change that,” Davis, who leads the Protecting Worship coalition, told JNS. “If the mayor’s new de-escalation unit can convince his own allies to stop targeting houses of worship, we’ll all welcome it.”

Jim Geraghty, senior political correspondent at National Review, addressed the Mamdani decision on his podcast “Three Martini Lunch.”

“You’ve basically announced this is your permission slip,” he said. “This doesn’t work in other cities. Why it would work in New York is completely beyond me, but it feels very on brand for Mamdani to say, ‘I’m going to do everything I can to make my city feel more chaotic and more like an angry mob is really in control.’”

آماده‌سازی برای نخستین دیدار سه‌جانبه رهبران چین، روسیه و آمریکا در تاریخ، در اروپا نگرانی‌هایی را برانگیخته است؛ جایی که برخی آن را یادآور تقسیم جهان به حوزه‌های نفوذ پس از جنگ جهانی دوم می‌دانند.

ولادیمیر پوتین، رئیس‌جمهوری روسیه، روز ۴ نوامبر هنگام بازدید از نمایشگاهی در مانژ مسکو در میدان سرخ، همراه گروهی از دانش‌آموزان، مقابل مجسمه بزرگی از وینستون چرچیل، نخست‌وزیر وقت بریتانیا، فرانکلین دی روزولت، رئیس‌جمهوری آمریکا، و ژوزف استالین، رهبر اتحاد جماهیر شوروی، در کنفرانس یالتا در فوریه ۱۹۴۵ توقف کرد.

پوتین به کودکان گفت: «این‌ها رهبران سه قدرت اصلی بودند که گرد هم آمدند تا درباره این‌که جهان پس از جنگ چگونه باید سازمان‌دهی شود گفت‌وگو کنند.»

نشست میان پوتین، دونالد ترامپ، رئیس‌جمهوری آمریکا، و شی جین‌پینگ، رئیس‌جمهوری چین، در روزهای ۱۸ و ۱۹ نوامبر دیدار می‌کنند؛ زمانی که هر سه برای اجلاس همکاری اقتصادی آسیا-اقیانوسیه، موسوم به «اپک»، در شنژن حضور خواهند داشت. اولیویا ولز، سخنگوی کاخ سفید، تایید کرد که این دیدار برگزار خواهد شد.

وقتی نخستین گزارش‌ها درباره پیشنهاد کرملین برای چنین دیداری در اواسط اکتبر منتشر شد، بلافاصله در اتحادیه اروپا و اوکراین نگرانی ایجاد کرد و برای بسیاری یادآور نشست رهبران ائتلاف ضد هیتلر در یالتا، در اقامتگاه سابق تزارهای روسیه در ساحل دریای سیاه، شد.

روزولت و چرچیل توانستند استالین را متقاعد کنند که پس از شکست آلمان وارد جنگ علیه ژاپن شود.

در مقابل، گسترش حوزه نفوذ اتحاد جماهیر شوروی در اروپای شرقی پذیرفته شد و توافقی محرمانه درباره شرق آسیا نیز صورت گرفت که طبق آن شوروی سرزمین‌های ژاپنی ساخالین جنوبی و جزایر کوریل را به دست می‌آورد، پایگاه شوروی در پورت‌آرتور چین احیا می‌شد و منافع اقتصادی ویژه‌ای برای شوروی در منچوری به رسمیت شناخته می‌شد.

از آن زمان، در اروپای شرقی، «یالتا» اغلب به تعبیری کوتاه برای یک معامله بدبینانه میان قدرت‌های بزرگ تبدیل شده است؛ معامله‌ای که جهان را بدون توجه به کشورهای کوچک‌تر، از جمله کشورهایی که قلمروشان میان قدرت‌ها تقسیم می‌شد، به حوزه‌های نفوذ تقسیم می‌کند.

ولودیمیر زلنسکی، رئیس‌جمهوری اوکراین، در واکنش گفت: «واقعا نمی‌خواهم این نشست به یالتا-۲، ۳ یا ۴ تبدیل شود و حوزه‌های نفوذ بین قدرت‌ها دوباره تقسیم شود.»

او افزود: «پس از آلاسکا، اگر رویدادها مطابق آنچه مقام‌های روسیه اکنون در چارچوب خواسته‌شان برای یک «یالتای» جدید مطرح می‌کنند پیش برود، این می‌تواند به دومین پیروزی بزرگ دیپلماتیک روسیه تبدیل شود.»

فریدریش مرتس، صدراعظم آلمان، گفته است مذاکرات برای پایان دادن به جنگ اوکراین باید با مشارکت اروپا انجام شود.

او گفت: «اروپا باید و می‌خواهد در این روند نقش داشته باشد. مسائل کلیدی یک توافق صلح، چه تحریم‌ها و چه معماری امنیتی، تنها با حضور ما اروپایی‌ها قابل حل است. همه طرف‌ها نیز این را می‌دانند.»

گزیده‌ای از مهم‌ترین خبرها، گزارش‌های میدانی و گفت‌وگوهای اختصاصی را هر هفته در ایمیل خود دریافت کنید.

اما هرچند پوتین ممکن است واقعا در پی کسب حمایت برای پایان دادن به جنگ اوکراین با شرایطی مطلوب برای روسیه باشد، آن‌گونه که وال‌استریت جورنال گزارش داده است، هنوز روشن نیست او دقیقا می‌خواهد با ترامپ و شی درباره چه چیزهایی گفت‌وگو کند.

یوری اوشاکوف، دستیار رئیس‌جمهوری روسیه، گفت: «در حال حاضر فقط طرح‌های اولیه‌ای درباره موضوعاتی وجود دارد که می‌توان در چنین سطح بالایی و در چنین قالب غیرمعمولی درباره آن‌ها گفت‌وگو کرد. فکر می‌کنم اوکراین به شکلی مطرح خواهد شد.»

ترامپ اما تصور متفاوتی از دستور کار احتمالی این اجلاس دارد.

او گفته است حاضر است با پوتین و شی دیدار کند، اما نه برای مذاکره درباره اوکراین: «می‌توانیم دیدار کنیم تا درباره سلاح‌های هسته‌ای و خلع سلاح هسته‌ای گفت‌وگو کنیم.»

جوزف توریگیان، متخصص چین و دانشیار دانشگاه امریکن در واشنگتن، معتقد است چین نمی‌خواهد فعالانه وارد مذاکرات مربوط به جنگ اوکراین شود، چون این کار این تصور را ایجاد می‌کند که پکن عمیقا در این درگیری دخیل است.

به گفته او، مشارکت در مذاکراتی که اروپا از آن کنار گذاشته شده باشد نیز به این برداشت دامن می‌زند که پکن در این جنگ از مسکو حمایت می‌کند؛ برداشتی که چین به‌شدت تلاش می‌کند از آن دوری کند.

این کارشناس می‌گوید پکن به مذاکرات درباره تسلیحات هسته‌ای نیز با تردید نگاه می‌کند.

او می‌گوید: «یکی از دلایل این است که روسیه و آمریکا زرادخانه‌های هسته‌ای به‌مراتب بزرگ‌تری از چین دارند. دلیل دیگر این است که چینی‌ها در مبهم بودن زرادخانه نسبتا کوچک هسته‌ای خود نوعی مزیت می‌بینند. آن‌ها ترجیح می‌دهند کشورهای دیگر از ابعاد دقیق برنامه هسته‌ای‌شان اطلاع نداشته باشند.»

منافع روسیه از چنین دیداری روشن است. نه فقط کنار گذاشتن اروپا از مذاکرات مربوط به جنگ اوکراین، بلکه نشان دادن دوباره این‌ که نمی‌توان مسکو را در عرصه بین‌المللی منزوی کرد.

جذابیت چنین دیداری برای رهبر آمریکا نیز روشن است.

توریگیان می‌گوید: «ترامپ بیش از هر چیز از جنبه تشریفاتی و فضای سیاسی این ایده هیجان‌زده است. او می‌تواند بگوید چقدر فوق‌العاده است که قدرت‌های بزرگ کنار هم جمع شده‌اند، این او بوده که برای نخستین بار توانسته چنین دیداری را ترتیب دهد و این‌که او صلح را برای جهان به ارمغان می‌آورد.»

اما مزایای چنین اجلاسی برای پکن بسیار کمتر روشن است.

توریگیان یادآوری می‌کند که کنفرانس یالتا فقط برای اروپای شرقی خاطره‌ای دردناک نیست، برای چین نیز چنین است، چون سرنوشت این کشور آن زمان توسط رهبران بریتانیا، شوروی و آمریکا و بدون مشارکت خود چین تعیین می‌شد.

استالین برای ورود شوروی به جنگ علیه ژاپن شروط سختی مطرح کرده بود، از جمله این‌ که مسکو موفق شد منافع ویژه شوروی در منچوری را به رسمیت بشناساند.

زمانی که رهبران چین از این مسئله با خبر شدند، خشمگین شدند.

توریگیان می‌گوید: «حتی مائو تسه‌تونگ، پس از پیروزی کمونیست‌ها در چین در سال ۱۹۴۹، خواسته‌های شوروی در یالتا و پس از آن را منبع جدی اختلاف می‌دانست. این اختلاف‌ها تا حدی شکاف بعدی میان چین و شوروی را نیز توضیح می‌دهد. بنابراین برای چینی‌ها، یالتا اصلا خاطره تاریخی خوشایندی نیست.»

در مورد اروپای شرقی، تاریخ‌نگاران هنوز درباره این موضوع بحث می‌کنند که گسترش حوزه نفوذ شوروی تا چه اندازه صرفا پذیرش واقعیتی اجتناب‌ناپذیر بود. تا فوریه ۱۹۴۵، ارتش سرخ از پیش رومانی، بلغارستان و بخش‌های بزرگی از لهستان، مجارستان و چکسلواکی را در اشغال داشت.

اما امروز ارتش روسیه حتی همه سرزمین‌های شرق اوکراین را که کرملین پیش‌تر بخشی از روسیه اعلام کرده است، در کنترل ندارد و برخلاف سال ۱۹۴۵، فقط یکی از شرکت‌کنندگان احتمالی این نشست مستقیما در جنگ دخیل است.

توریگیان می‌گوید روسیه همچنین تنها کشوری است که همچنان به تقسیم روشن جهان به حوزه‌های نفوذ علاقه دارد.

اگرچه راهبرد امنیت ملی تصویب‌شده در دوره ترامپ، نیمکره غربی را حوزه نفوذ آمریکا توصیف می‌کند، ایالات متحده آماده نیست حمایت خود از تایوان را کنار بگذارد. حضور چین در آمریکای لاتین نیز همچنان برای پکن اهمیت دارد.

روسیه خود را ابرقدرتی هم‌تراز آمریکا و چین می‌داند و در بیانیه‌های رسمی چین نیز اغلب از روسیه به‌عنوان کشوری هم‌سطح یاد می‌شود.

اما مارسین کاچمارسکی از دانشگاه گلاسگو می‌گوید: «پشت درهای بسته، نه کارشناسان چینی و نه رهبران چین، روسیه را قدرتی برابر با خودشان نمی‌دانند.»

او می‌گوید: «تنها کشوری که رهبران و نخبگان چین واقعا آن را هم‌تراز چین می‌دانند، ایالات متحده است.»

کاچمارسکی می‌گوید یک نشست سه‌جانبه می‌تواند اعتبار بین‌المللی پکن را افزایش دهد و شی را در جایگاه یک دولتمرد جهانی نشان دهد که رهبران دیگر قدرت‌های بزرگ برای دیدارش نزد او می‌آیند.

اما از سوی دیگر، به گفته او، چین به ناراحتی احتمالی اروپا از چنین دیداری نیازی ندارد.

اگرچه نخبگان چین در سال‌های اخیر با احترام کمتری به اتحادیه اروپا نگاه می‌کنند، همچنان به حفظ روابط خوب با کشورهای اروپایی به‌عنوان شرکای تجاری کلیدی علاقه‌مندند.

اما موقعیت ترامپ در صحنه جهانی نیز پس از شکست جمهوری‌خواهان در انتخابات میان‌دوره‌ای کنگره آمریکا نامطمئن‌تر شده است.

کاچمارسکی می‌گوید: «سوال این است که آیا چین علاقه دارد به تقویت جایگاه بین‌المللی [ترامپ] کمک کند؟»

در دهه ۲۰۰۰، جورج دبلیو بوش، رئیس‌جمهوری وقت آمریکا، هنگام سفر به اروپای شرقی چند بار توافق‌های یالتا را یک شر تاریخی خواند.

نیویورک تایمز در آن زمان نوشته بود مخاطب اصلی این پیام‌ها رهبر روسیه بود.

بوش به پوتین پیام می‌داد که روسیه حق ندارد در امور همسایگانش مداخله کند و باید بابت اقدامات اتحاد جماهیر شوروی عذرخواهی کند. او در سال ۲۰۰۲ در ویلنیوس اعلام کرد: «دیگر هیچ یالتایی در کار نیست!»

اگر ۲۵ سال بعد، پوتین بتواند رهبران آمریکا و چین را به دیداری در قالبی وادارد که حتی از دور یادآور کنفرانس یالتا باشد، این برای رهبر روسیه یک پیروزی نمادین خواهد بود حتی اگر این دیدار هیچ محتوای مشخصی نداشته باشد.

آماده‌سازی برای نخستین دیدار سه‌جانبه رهبران چین، روسیه و آمریکا در تاریخ، در اروپا نگرانی‌هایی را برانگیخته است؛ جایی که برخی آن را یادآور تقسیم جهان به حوزه‌های نفوذ پس از جنگ جهانی دوم می‌دانند.

ولادیمیر پوتین، رئیس‌جمهوری روسیه، روز ۴ نوامبر هنگام بازدید از نمایشگاهی در مانژ مسکو در میدان سرخ، همراه گروهی از دانش‌آموزان، مقابل مجسمه بزرگی از وینستون چرچیل، نخست‌وزیر وقت بریتانیا، فرانکلین دی روزولت، رئیس‌جمهوری آمریکا، و ژوزف استالین، رهبر اتحاد جماهیر شوروی، در کنفرانس یالتا در فوریه ۱۹۴۵ توقف کرد.

پوتین به کودکان گفت: «این‌ها رهبران سه قدرت اصلی بودند که گرد هم آمدند تا درباره این‌که جهان پس از جنگ چگونه باید سازمان‌دهی شود گفت‌وگو کنند.»

نشست میان پوتین، دونالد ترامپ، رئیس‌جمهوری آمریکا، و شی جین‌پینگ، رئیس‌جمهوری چین، در روزهای ۱۸ و ۱۹ نوامبر دیدار می‌کنند؛ زمانی که هر سه برای اجلاس همکاری اقتصادی آسیا-اقیانوسیه، موسوم به «اپک»، در شنژن حضور خواهند داشت. اولیویا ولز، سخنگوی کاخ سفید، تایید کرد که این دیدار برگزار خواهد شد.

وقتی نخستین گزارش‌ها درباره پیشنهاد کرملین برای چنین دیداری در اواسط اکتبر منتشر شد، بلافاصله در اتحادیه اروپا و اوکراین نگرانی ایجاد کرد و برای بسیاری یادآور نشست رهبران ائتلاف ضد هیتلر در یالتا، در اقامتگاه سابق تزارهای روسیه در ساحل دریای سیاه، شد.

روزولت و چرچیل توانستند استالین را متقاعد کنند که پس از شکست آلمان وارد جنگ علیه ژاپن شود.

در مقابل، گسترش حوزه نفوذ اتحاد جماهیر شوروی در اروپای شرقی پذیرفته شد و توافقی محرمانه درباره شرق آسیا نیز صورت گرفت که طبق آن شوروی سرزمین‌های ژاپنی ساخالین جنوبی و جزایر کوریل را به دست می‌آورد، پایگاه شوروی در پورت‌آرتور چین احیا می‌شد و منافع اقتصادی ویژه‌ای برای شوروی در منچوری به رسمیت شناخته می‌شد.

از آن زمان، در اروپای شرقی، «یالتا» اغلب به تعبیری کوتاه برای یک معامله بدبینانه میان قدرت‌های بزرگ تبدیل شده است؛ معامله‌ای که جهان را بدون توجه به کشورهای کوچک‌تر، از جمله کشورهایی که قلمروشان میان قدرت‌ها تقسیم می‌شد، به حوزه‌های نفوذ تقسیم می‌کند.

ولودیمیر زلنسکی، رئیس‌جمهوری اوکراین، در واکنش گفت: «واقعا نمی‌خواهم این نشست به یالتا-۲، ۳ یا ۴ تبدیل شود و حوزه‌های نفوذ بین قدرت‌ها دوباره تقسیم شود.»

او افزود: «پس از آلاسکا، اگر رویدادها مطابق آنچه مقام‌های روسیه اکنون در چارچوب خواسته‌شان برای یک «یالتای» جدید مطرح می‌کنند پیش برود، این می‌تواند به دومین پیروزی بزرگ دیپلماتیک روسیه تبدیل شود.»

فریدریش مرتس، صدراعظم آلمان، گفته است مذاکرات برای پایان دادن به جنگ اوکراین باید با مشارکت اروپا انجام شود.

او گفت: «اروپا باید و می‌خواهد در این روند نقش داشته باشد. مسائل کلیدی یک توافق صلح، چه تحریم‌ها و چه معماری امنیتی، تنها با حضور ما اروپایی‌ها قابل حل است. همه طرف‌ها نیز این را می‌دانند.»

گزیده‌ای از مهم‌ترین خبرها، گزارش‌های میدانی و گفت‌وگوهای اختصاصی را هر هفته در ایمیل خود دریافت کنید.

اما هرچند پوتین ممکن است واقعا در پی کسب حمایت برای پایان دادن به جنگ اوکراین با شرایطی مطلوب برای روسیه باشد، آن‌گونه که وال‌استریت جورنال گزارش داده است، هنوز روشن نیست او دقیقا می‌خواهد با ترامپ و شی درباره چه چیزهایی گفت‌وگو کند.

یوری اوشاکوف، دستیار رئیس‌جمهوری روسیه، گفت: «در حال حاضر فقط طرح‌های اولیه‌ای درباره موضوعاتی وجود دارد که می‌توان در چنین سطح بالایی و در چنین قالب غیرمعمولی درباره آن‌ها گفت‌وگو کرد. فکر می‌کنم اوکراین به شکلی مطرح خواهد شد.»

ترامپ اما تصور متفاوتی از دستور کار احتمالی این اجلاس دارد.

او گفته است حاضر است با پوتین و شی دیدار کند، اما نه برای مذاکره درباره اوکراین: «می‌توانیم دیدار کنیم تا درباره سلاح‌های هسته‌ای و خلع سلاح هسته‌ای گفت‌وگو کنیم.»

جوزف توریگیان، متخصص چین و دانشیار دانشگاه امریکن در واشنگتن، معتقد است چین نمی‌خواهد فعالانه وارد مذاکرات مربوط به جنگ اوکراین شود، چون این کار این تصور را ایجاد می‌کند که پکن عمیقا در این درگیری دخیل است.

به گفته او، مشارکت در مذاکراتی که اروپا از آن کنار گذاشته شده باشد نیز به این برداشت دامن می‌زند که پکن در این جنگ از مسکو حمایت می‌کند؛ برداشتی که چین به‌شدت تلاش می‌کند از آن دوری کند.

این کارشناس می‌گوید پکن به مذاکرات درباره تسلیحات هسته‌ای نیز با تردید نگاه می‌کند.

او می‌گوید: «یکی از دلایل این است که روسیه و آمریکا زرادخانه‌های هسته‌ای به‌مراتب بزرگ‌تری از چین دارند. دلیل دیگر این است که چینی‌ها در مبهم بودن زرادخانه نسبتا کوچک هسته‌ای خود نوعی مزیت می‌بینند. آن‌ها ترجیح می‌دهند کشورهای دیگر از ابعاد دقیق برنامه هسته‌ای‌شان اطلاع نداشته باشند.»

منافع روسیه از چنین دیداری روشن است. نه فقط کنار گذاشتن اروپا از مذاکرات مربوط به جنگ اوکراین، بلکه نشان دادن دوباره این‌ که نمی‌توان مسکو را در عرصه بین‌المللی منزوی کرد.

جذابیت چنین دیداری برای رهبر آمریکا نیز روشن است.

توریگیان می‌گوید: «ترامپ بیش از هر چیز از جنبه تشریفاتی و فضای سیاسی این ایده هیجان‌زده است. او می‌تواند بگوید چقدر فوق‌العاده است که قدرت‌های بزرگ کنار هم جمع شده‌اند، این او بوده که برای نخستین بار توانسته چنین دیداری را ترتیب دهد و این‌که او صلح را برای جهان به ارمغان می‌آورد.»

اما مزایای چنین اجلاسی برای پکن بسیار کمتر روشن است.

توریگیان یادآوری می‌کند که کنفرانس یالتا فقط برای اروپای شرقی خاطره‌ای دردناک نیست، برای چین نیز چنین است، چون سرنوشت این کشور آن زمان توسط رهبران بریتانیا، شوروی و آمریکا و بدون مشارکت خود چین تعیین می‌شد.

استالین برای ورود شوروی به جنگ علیه ژاپن شروط سختی مطرح کرده بود، از جمله این‌ که مسکو موفق شد منافع ویژه شوروی در منچوری را به رسمیت بشناساند.

زمانی که رهبران چین از این مسئله با خبر شدند، خشمگین شدند.

توریگیان می‌گوید: «حتی مائو تسه‌تونگ، پس از پیروزی کمونیست‌ها در چین در سال ۱۹۴۹، خواسته‌های شوروی در یالتا و پس از آن را منبع جدی اختلاف می‌دانست. این اختلاف‌ها تا حدی شکاف بعدی میان چین و شوروی را نیز توضیح می‌دهد. بنابراین برای چینی‌ها، یالتا اصلا خاطره تاریخی خوشایندی نیست.»

در مورد اروپای شرقی، تاریخ‌نگاران هنوز درباره این موضوع بحث می‌کنند که گسترش حوزه نفوذ شوروی تا چه اندازه صرفا پذیرش واقعیتی اجتناب‌ناپذیر بود. تا فوریه ۱۹۴۵، ارتش سرخ از پیش رومانی، بلغارستان و بخش‌های بزرگی از لهستان، مجارستان و چکسلواکی را در اشغال داشت.

اما امروز ارتش روسیه حتی همه سرزمین‌های شرق اوکراین را که کرملین پیش‌تر بخشی از روسیه اعلام کرده است، در کنترل ندارد و برخلاف سال ۱۹۴۵، فقط یکی از شرکت‌کنندگان احتمالی این نشست مستقیما در جنگ دخیل است.

توریگیان می‌گوید روسیه همچنین تنها کشوری است که همچنان به تقسیم روشن جهان به حوزه‌های نفوذ علاقه دارد.

اگرچه راهبرد امنیت ملی تصویب‌شده در دوره ترامپ، نیمکره غربی را حوزه نفوذ آمریکا توصیف می‌کند، ایالات متحده آماده نیست حمایت خود از تایوان را کنار بگذارد. حضور چین در آمریکای لاتین نیز همچنان برای پکن اهمیت دارد.

روسیه خود را ابرقدرتی هم‌تراز آمریکا و چین می‌داند و در بیانیه‌های رسمی چین نیز اغلب از روسیه به‌عنوان کشوری هم‌سطح یاد می‌شود.

اما مارسین کاچمارسکی از دانشگاه گلاسگو می‌گوید: «پشت درهای بسته، نه کارشناسان چینی و نه رهبران چین، روسیه را قدرتی برابر با خودشان نمی‌دانند.»

او می‌گوید: «تنها کشوری که رهبران و نخبگان چین واقعا آن را هم‌تراز چین می‌دانند، ایالات متحده است.»

کاچمارسکی می‌گوید یک نشست سه‌جانبه می‌تواند اعتبار بین‌المللی پکن را افزایش دهد و شی را در جایگاه یک دولتمرد جهانی نشان دهد که رهبران دیگر قدرت‌های بزرگ برای دیدارش نزد او می‌آیند.

اما از سوی دیگر، به گفته او، چین به ناراحتی احتمالی اروپا از چنین دیداری نیازی ندارد.

اگرچه نخبگان چین در سال‌های اخیر با احترام کمتری به اتحادیه اروپا نگاه می‌کنند، همچنان به حفظ روابط خوب با کشورهای اروپایی به‌عنوان شرکای تجاری کلیدی علاقه‌مندند.

اما موقعیت ترامپ در صحنه جهانی نیز پس از شکست جمهوری‌خواهان در انتخابات میان‌دوره‌ای کنگره آمریکا نامطمئن‌تر شده است.

کاچمارسکی می‌گوید: «سوال این است که آیا چین علاقه دارد به تقویت جایگاه بین‌المللی [ترامپ] کمک کند؟»

در دهه ۲۰۰۰، جورج دبلیو بوش، رئیس‌جمهوری وقت آمریکا، هنگام سفر به اروپای شرقی چند بار توافق‌های یالتا را یک شر تاریخی خواند.

نیویورک تایمز در آن زمان نوشته بود مخاطب اصلی این پیام‌ها رهبر روسیه بود.

بوش به پوتین پیام می‌داد که روسیه حق ندارد در امور همسایگانش مداخله کند و باید بابت اقدامات اتحاد جماهیر شوروی عذرخواهی کند. او در سال ۲۰۰۲ در ویلنیوس اعلام کرد: «دیگر هیچ یالتایی در کار نیست!»

اگر ۲۵ سال بعد، پوتین بتواند رهبران آمریکا و چین را به دیداری در قالبی وادارد که حتی از دور یادآور کنفرانس یالتا باشد، این برای رهبر روسیه یک پیروزی نمادین خواهد بود حتی اگر این دیدار هیچ محتوای مشخصی نداشته باشد.

news.originalContent:
The ongoing student protests in France are a symptom of a much larger crisis affecting French society.

Fifty years ago, Alain Peyrefitte, who served as a spokesperson for French President Charles de Gaulle, published a book entitled Le Mal français (The French Malaise). In the book, Peyrefitte wrote that the progress of the French nation was impeded by the lack of trust – within society and between society and state institutions. In reaction, the state exercised excessive control through rules, bureaucracy and centralisation, which resulted in stagnation.

Today, the French malaise persists, but its symptoms are quite different from the ones observed by Peyrefitte. We now have the dramatic protests by French students as well as workers and other disaffected groups, which at times have turned violent.

But these demonstrations are only the tip of the iceberg. The malaise runs much deeper.

Following the events of October 17, in which symbols of state authority were attacked – including the town halls of Limoges and Marseille and an official building in Lyon – and businesses were looted, French President Emmanuel Macron stated that these acts sought “to tear down our institutions”.

The use of such strong words reminds one of the rhetoric employed by the French government during the protests of May 1968, when students challenged the established order, and their actions were portrayed as an “attack on the Republic”.

There is, in fact, a tendency to compare the current wave of demonstrations with the events of May 1968. Yet the two movements differ. The protesters of 1968 were calling for more freedom, while today’s protesters are demanding equality and dignity. The former demonstrations were led by privileged youth; the latter are driven by those who have been left behind.

Perhaps a more relevant episode to examine is the upheaval of 2005 in the suburbs of Paris and other major cities following the deaths of two teenagers, Bouna and Zyed, who were pursued by the police.

For three weeks, residents of impoverished neighbourhoods, living on the fringes of society both geographically and socially, expressed their anger at police violence and their own marginalisation.

Two elements of the French malaise were already apparent at the time. First was the deep divide between two segments of society: the prosperous urban population and the marginalised, racialised poor, living in the underdeveloped and underserviced outskirts.

The second was the French police itself, which has overwhelmingly focused on policing the latter with ever-growing brutality.

In any country, a citizen-oriented police force can help build the bonds that unite a nation. But in France, the police is tasked with defending the state, not protecting the citizens.

It does not contribute to the cohesion of a nation. It does not abide by proportionality in the use of force or opt for de-escalation; it openly practises a discriminatory approach to policing which differentiates between affluent neighbourhoods and impoverished areas, between the white majority and the communities of colour.

It is no wonder that upwards of 60 percent of the police and military forces of France vote for the far right.

In 2019, French political scientist Jérôme Fourquet wrote a book entitled The French Archipelago: The birth of a diverse and divided nation. In it, he argues that France has undergone a societal shift which has fundamentally altered people’s relationship with themselves and with the “other”. As a result, French society has split into small “islands” which are increasingly isolated from one another.

This transformation cannot be attributed solely to immigration. It is, above all, the result of the secession of the elite, which has grown distant and indifferent to the fate of the rest of the nation. This includes the political left, who are now commonly referred to as the gauche caviar (the caviar left).

It has been the elite’s abandonment and self-isolation that has caused the revolt of the masses, rather than the other way around.

The institutions that traditionally fostered socialisation between various groups, bestowing a sense of belonging, including schools, summer camps and compulsory military service, are no longer functioning effectively, or are cancelled.

In this fragmented society, one segment has been picked as a scapegoat for all problems, diverting attention from the real roots of the malaise.

Islamophobia is flourishing in France, as is the belief in the “Great Replacement”, a conspiracy theory that people of colour are meant to “replace” the white majority. Islamophobia has even become institutionalised through legislation and a political culture that has transformed blasphemy into something resembling a duty.

The paradox is that France – compared with its neighbours – has a smaller immigrant population while it espouses a much louder rhetoric about “integration”.

And there is a considerable gap between rhetoric and reality. While those in power demand that people of immigrant background “integrate”, very little is done by the state to actually drive this process.

As a result, some French citizens feel they are French only on paper. They understand that citizenship cannot be reduced to a political discourse. Without genuine access to rights, which necessarily entails social justice and human dignity, there can be no meaningful citizenship.

In 2005, a group of activists went as far as declaring themselves the “Natives of the Republic” and calling for its decolonisation. Indeed, anyone familiar with French society can recognise that France has reproduced a colonial order within.

The country that gave birth to the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen has failed to treat some of its own people as full citizens. And that stands at the core of the new French malaise.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

For three weeks, residents of impoverished neighbourhoods, living on the fringes of society both geographically and socially, expressed their anger at police violence and their own marginalisation.

Two elements of the French malaise were already apparent at the time. First was the deep divide between two segments of society: the prosperous urban population and the marginalised, racialised poor, living in the underdeveloped and underserviced outskirts.

The second was the French police itself, which has overwhelmingly focused on policing the latter with ever-growing brutality.

In any country, a citizen-oriented police force can help build the bonds that unite a nation. But in France, the police is tasked with defending the state, not protecting the citizens.

It does not contribute to the cohesion of a nation. It does not abide by proportionality in the use of force or opt for de-escalation; it openly practises a discriminatory approach to policing which differentiates between affluent neighbourhoods and impoverished areas, between the white majority and the communities of colour.

It is no wonder that upwards of 60 percent of the police and military forces of France vote for the far right.

In 2019, French political scientist Jérôme Fourquet wrote a book entitled The French Archipelago: The birth of a diverse and divided nation. In it, he argues that France has undergone a societal shift which has fundamentally altered people’s relationship with themselves and with the “other”. As a result, French society has split into small “islands” which are increasingly isolated from one another.

This transformation cannot be attributed solely to immigration. It is, above all, the result of the secession of the elite, which has grown distant and indifferent to the fate of the rest of the nation. This includes the political left, who are now commonly referred to as the gauche caviar (the caviar left).

It has been the elite’s abandonment and self-isolation that has caused the revolt of the masses, rather than the other way around.

The institutions that traditionally fostered socialisation between various groups, bestowing a sense of belonging, including schools, summer camps and compulsory military service, are no longer functioning effectively, or are cancelled.

In this fragmented society, one segment has been picked as a scapegoat for all problems, diverting attention from the real roots of the malaise.

Islamophobia is flourishing in France, as is the belief in the “Great Replacement”, a conspiracy theory that people of colour are meant to “replace” the white majority. Islamophobia has even become institutionalised through legislation and a political culture that has transformed blasphemy into something resembling a duty.

The paradox is that France – compared with its neighbours – has a smaller immigrant population while it espouses a much louder rhetoric about “integration”.

And there is a considerable gap between rhetoric and reality. While those in power demand that people of immigrant background “integrate”, very little is done by the state to actually drive this process.

As a result, some French citizens feel they are French only on paper. They understand that citizenship cannot be reduced to a political discourse. Without genuine access to rights, which necessarily entails social justice and human dignity, there can be no meaningful citizenship.

In 2005, a group of activists went as far as declaring themselves the “Natives of the Republic” and calling for its decolonisation. Indeed, anyone familiar with French society can recognise that France has reproduced a colonial order within.

The country that gave birth to the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen has failed to treat some of its own people as full citizens. And that stands at the core of the new French malaise.

Teresa Giudice is spilling the tea on a “rude” interaction she once had with “a well-known actress.”

In her new memoir, “The Queen of New Jersey,” out now, the Bravo star recalls a time when her PR team allegedly had her pose with the celebrity while in Los Angeles for an appearance with Mario Lopez.

After they took a photo together, Giudice claims the female actress — whose name she did not reveal — asked her reps, “Why are you making me take a picture with that woman?”

Giudice, 54, went on to recall the actress having a “surprising” tone when she made the alleged comment.

“Look, I get if she didn’t know who I was, but to me, that’s just so rude,” the “Real Housewives of New Jersey” star writes.

Giudice adds that a few years later, she and her husband, Louie “Luis” Ruelas, were having dinner in LA when a girl walked in and asked the reality star for a picture.

Ten minutes later, the actress walked into the same restaurant.

“We made brief eye contact — there was definitely no need to say hi — as she was shown to her table,” Giudice writes.

Ironically, the actress was meeting the girl who had just fangirled over Giudice.

“I hope she enjoyed feigning interest as her friend showed her the pictures we’d taken just moments before,” Giudice says.

The mom of four notes that as someone in the public eye, she can’t stand stars who are publicly rude to fans.

“There are a lot of people in this business who can’t stand to stop and pose for a photo or sign something for a fan. Like, really?” she writes. “You think you’re such a big deal that you can’t spare a moment for the very audience whose attention made you who you are?”

Later in her book, Giudice, who has been on television since 2009, says fans are her “real boss.”

“I’ll admit that sometimes people take things too far and get a little too obsessed or invasive,” she acknowledges. “Everyone has to have some sort of boundary, and there’s a level of human decency that should apply to your interactions with any person, no matter how famous.”

Giudice adds, “But for the most part, my fans really are the loveliest people. I’ve met fans all over the world, and it is always the best part of my job.”

Giudice also revisits “the biggest triumphs, heartbreaks, feuds and controversies of her life with newfound perspective” in “The Queen of New Jersey,” according to an official description for the memoir.

She writes about everything from her divorce with ex-husband Joe Giudice and his deportation to her father’s death, her love story with Ruelas and more.

“The Queen of New Jersey” is out now.

news.originalContent:
The Israeli prime minister has manoeuvred out of tough situations before to retain power. But he may find it hard this time.

Akiva Eldar is an Israeli author and was formerly an editorial writer and columnist for Haaretz.

I have been covering Benjamin Netanyahu for more than 30 years. I was in Washington when, as a young opposition leader, he worked hand in glove with the Republicans to embarrass Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and sabotage the Oslo Accords. I have seen him cornered before. I have never seen him cornered like this.

The numbers are merciless. His bloc won 53 seats, eight short of a majority. Sixty-seven members of the new Knesset recommended former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, who now has up to 42 days to form a government. For Netanyahu, they may be the longest 42 days of his political life.

The stakes are political, but above all personal. His corruption trial continues, and he faces a possible prison sentence. His pardon request has been gathering dust on President Isaac Herzog’s desk for months. Eisenkot’s bloc has already tabled bills for a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 attacks and for prime-ministerial term limits.

A state inquiry would strip him of the title he covets the most: “defender of Israel”. For Netanyahu, the chair is not a job. It is a lifeline. His trial, under way since May 2020, is in its final stretch. A sitting prime minister can be removed only after a final conviction.

From his office, he can stall hearings and lean on the justice system. Out of office, he is just another defendant.

To survive, Netanyahu does not need to build a government. He needs time to keep his rivals from building one. To buy it, he is pulling three levers.

The first is his proposal for a “national unity government” of all the parties that support Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people. Translation: the Arab parties, representing 21 percent of the population, are out. The Jewish supremacists, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, are in. So are the anti-Zionist Haredi parties. This is unity, Netanyahu-style.

He has gift-wrapped the offer in the old rhetoric of the Iranian nuclear threat, with one catch: He would not give up the premiership or agree to a rotation.

Eisenkot has called the offer “another spin”, yet he has agreed to negotiate with Likud. He knows a refusal would only feed the spin machine: They will talk to Arab supporters of Hamas, but not to Jewish patriots, the Netanyahu camp would claim.

He also knows to beware of a diversion designed to burn through the days the president has allotted him.

The second lever is incitement. At the Knesset’s opening session, Netanyahu branded Ra’am and the Joint List “terror supporters” and “haters of Israel”. A government depending on them, he declared, “must not be formed”. The goal is to strangle an Arab-backed government in its cradle, and to scare the Haredi parties, which are currently part of his bloc, away from joining the “enemy”.

But this time the incitement has a hole in it. Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas says Netanyahu’s confidant Natan Eshel sounded him out on the bill to bar an indicted politician from serving as prime minister. Joint List lawmaker Ahmad Tibi went on live television with WhatsApp messages he said came from Eshel. “Terror supporters”, it seems, are good enough for a quiet chat.

The third lever is escalation. According to media reports, Netanyahu has been pressing US President Donald Trump for another wave of strikes on Iran. A return to full-scale war could help him form an emergency government.

In a media interview, former Prime Minister Ehud Barak laid out the scenario: a blatant provocation that forces Iran to respond, and a war that would disrupt or prevent the establishment of a new government. Lebanon, Gaza or the West Bank could serve just as well. The mantra is well-known: The enemy must see that we are united.

Here, too, there are limits. A former chief of staff of the army, Eisenkot spent many years in uniform and has no shortage of sources in the army. They are likely telling him there is no urgent need for another round of war with Iran. And Trump has hinted that he wants that war over.

If all three levers fail, Netanyahu has a familiar fallback: another election, next spring. Between 2019 and 2022, he dragged Israelis to the polls five times rather than give up the chair. Tibi has revealed that one of Netanyahu’s ministers tried to convince him his party would be better off “going to elections” than joining Eisenkot’s bloc.

Eisenkot has a problem of his own. He campaigned on three pledges: no Netanyahu, no Haredi parties, no Arab parties. He cannot keep all three. Politics is the art of choosing which promise to break.

The first path available to Eisenkot runs through the Haredim. His bloc has 48 seats; Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ) would add 13, for exactly 61, the number he needs to secure a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. A softened draft law is reportedly on the table. But UTJ’s rabbis want all 48 members of the bloc to sign a pledge exempting Haredim from military service, with an override clause to shield the law from the Supreme Court. Eisenkot has pledged not to back down on military service for all.

The second path is a minority government, backed by the Arab parties from outside the coalition. Eisenkot is reportedly willing to do it, and so is one of his allies, Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats. Another ally, Naftali Bennett, is believed to oppose it. The big obstacle is Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Lieberman, who rules out the Arab parties, a minority government and new elections. Three noes in a single breath.

The third path is Likud without Netanyahu, or with him in a diplomatic role. No Likud lawmaker has broken ranks so far. And for Netanyahu, a junior partnership would be not a retirement plan but a launching pad: From inside the cabinet, he could stall the bills on a state inquiry and term limits, undermine the government and bring it down at a moment of his choosing. Just ask Benny Gantz, whose 2020 rotation deal with Netanyahu never brought him to the prime minister’s chair.

This is a game of chicken. Netanyahu is betting that Eisenkot’s partners will squabble over the draft, the Arab parties and the portfolios until the clock runs out, forcing a seventh election since 2019 — one he would fight from the Prime Minister’s Office, his finger on the trigger. Eisenkot’s best weapon is the one Netanyahu fears the most: a government, any government, sworn in before the 42 days are up.

Eisenkot’s camp has already taken over the Knesset building. Netanyahu’s camp will do everything it can to keep it from taking over the government buildings. They will not give up without street battles.

The last time incitement spilled into the streets, in November 1995, it ended with the assassination of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin. It paved the way for the comeback of the Israeli right, led by a young, charming Revisionist.

Will November 2026 mark the end of the Netanyahu era and a return to Rabin’s path of peace?

The US curre
news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

The dollar on Tuesday ​scaled a fresh 19-month peak against a basket of peers amid bets for more ‌aggressive policy tightening by the US Federal Reserve following hot inflation data and hawkish central bank rhetoric.

The US currency extended a 10-month high versus its Australian counterpart as a global selloff in AI stocks weighed on market sentiment, hurting ​the risk-sensitive Aussie.

A sharper-than-expected acceleration in US consumer inflation last week triggered a run of ​five straight days of gains for the US dollar index , which carried into a ⁠sixth day on Tuesday with it rising to 103.66, the highest since April 2, 2025, when ​President Trump rolled out his tariffs.

The index measures the dollar against six rivals, including the ​euro, sterling and the Japanese yen.

Traders now view a Fed interest-rate hike at the next meeting in December as a certainty, and they also lay around 4% odds on a supersized half-point increase, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool. ​

A day earlier, those bets on an oversized hike were at nearly 12%. A week earlier, ​there were 16% odds for no change to policy.

Meanwhile, the tech selloff continued in Asia on Tuesday, with Japan’s Nikkei and ⁠South Korea’s KOSPI both firmly lower.

A key test for AI sentiment — which has been rocked by the sudden departure of Nvidia’s CEO, a Democratic sweep in US midterm elections and worries about a debt-fueled AI infrastructure expansion — comes with the release of Nvidia earnings later in the day.

The dollar has been ​supported by the AI ​boom as capital flowed ⁠into US markets.

“Continued AI-related capital inflows and expectations of faster Fed tightening should support the USD,” said CBA economist and currency strategist Carol Kong.

“However, erratic ​US policymaking and a sharp correction in AI-related equities pose key downside risks ​to our ⁠bullish USD outlook.”

In terms of the Fed outlook, US retail sales data later in the day could offer further clues.

The dollar edged to a fresh 18-month high of 0.84075 Swiss franc and rose slightly to 159.49 ⁠yen .

Japan’s currency ​has been hemmed in around 160 per dollar, which traders ​view as a potential trigger level for another round of intervention to support it.

The euro slipped to a new 19-month low ​of $1.0985. Sterling fell to $1.3172.

The Aussie dipped to $0.6725, the lowest since January.

As Eisenkot’s bloc moves to form a government and courts the ultra-Orthodox, the Gaza genocide and settler pogroms continue.

Israel’s parliament speaker is due to be replaced on Tuesday, one of several signs that power is being rearranged as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s bloc angles to lead the government.

But for Palestinians, the machinery of occupation, dispossession and deprivation keeps running. Israeli attacks killed at least 37 people in Gaza in the past week, while in the occupied West Bank, settlers attacked whole villages with little to stop them.

The past week saw numerous Israeli attacks and killings in Gaza, as military claims of targeting fighters were weighed against accounts of people killed in tents, filling water containers and driving to a wedding photo shoot. According to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, as of November 16, Israel has killed 1,650 Palestinians since the October 2025 “ceasefire”.

On November 12, an Israeli bomb hit the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis. The hospital’s surgery building was struck, killing six people, including surgeon Rizq Abu Shaira, and wounding dozens. The Israeli military said it targeted Hamas’s Khan Younis Brigade commander, Muhammad Abu Ismail, and accused Hamas of running a command centre in the hospital. In the days that followed, the foreign ministers of 18 Arab and Muslim-majority countries condemned the attack as a violation of international humanitarian law.

Beyond the hospital bombing, the Israeli military told Israeli media it had killed 10 Hamas operatives in the past week. Among them was Samir Abu Younis, whom the army named as Hamas’s Rafah Brigade commander, killed in a drone strike in al-Mawasi on November 14, which Hamas confirmed. The strike hit a tent for displaced people, wounding two. Over the weekend, in Jabalia camp, two men were killed in a strike the army said targeted “terrorists”, and a separate strike on a Gaza government security post in al-Mawasi, Rafah, killed two people, according to Wafa.

At the same time, Israeli forces continued to kill Palestinians in circumstances that offered little indication of any military target:

This week, Gaza’s Health Ministry recorded the winter’s first death from hypothermia – a nine-month-old baby – following the devastation of last week’s rains. Israel’s Prime Minister’s Office claimed more than 91,000 tents and 8,200 trucks of winter supplies have been delivered, the Times of Israel reported, and blamed Hamas for the suffering. The United Nations, however, reported this week that aid-truck offloads have fallen about 42 percent after Israel suspended the Egyptian corridor.

The United Kingdom, Australia, Canada and Italy called conditions in Gaza “catastrophic” and urged that 150,000 tents be allowed into the territory.

The most violent olive harvest on record continues in the occupied West Bank, as OCHA counted 410 harvest-related attacks this year as of November 9. The week saw several kinds of attacks by settlers and soldiers unfold repeatedly across the West Bank:

But in the past week, two settler attacks escalated into full-blown pogroms against Palestinian communities. Late on November 10, more than 50 masked settlers set fire to a scrapyard, a workshop and cars beside homes in al-Lubban Asharqiya, south of Nablus, burning more than 100 vehicles and dozens of olive trees and cutting power. Wafa put the damage from the attack at more than one million shekels ($310,000). On November 12, after soldiers evicted an outpost near Atara, north of Ramallah, settlers smashed four homes and a factory and wrecked at least three cars, injuring more than 10 residents.

The Israeli army evacuated outposts near Burqa, Wadi al-Rakhim and Jalud, and on November 11, police arrested four Israelis over a September attack by settlers on troops escorting a displaced Palestinian family, the Times of Israel reported.

Yet settlers re-established an outpost at Burqa within days, and in Wadi al-Rakhim, south of Yatta, the six-week siege of Yousef Shanaran’s home by settlers continues unimpeded. While soldiers pulled down the settlers’ tent outside Shanaran’s home on November 13, the tent was rebuilt after sunset, according to the family. On November 16, Shanaran told Al Jazeera that settlers had thrown stones at their home throughout the previous night. Soldiers were present, but did nothing. “We are alone,” he declared.

As the occupation continues largely unchecked, early coalition negotiations suggest that a change of government might mean little more than a rearrangement of the political chairs for Palestinians. On November 10, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told the new parliament in a speech Eisenkot called “hate-filled” that Arab-led parties “seek to destroy the Jewish state”, while demanding a Zionist unity government instead of the opposition partnering with the parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Meanwhile, Israel’s Channel 12 reported on November 15 that Netanyahu’s chief of staff had given police the tip behind three election-day arrests of activists from Ra’am, one of the Arab-led parties. Israel’s attorney general is probing whether Netanyahu’s office engineered the case to bolster claims that Arab parties stole the vote. Shin Bet chief David Zini also asked to wiretap five Palestinian members of the Israeli parliament, Channel 12 reported. Netanyahu’s office has called the report defamatory.

Eisenkot called the campaign against Palestinian citizens of Israel “racist and violent” and said Netanyahu was a threat to Israeli democracy who could not stay “for even one more minute”.

Yet he has ruled out a government with the Arab parties, whose 19 seats would give his bloc 67, above the 61-seat majority threshold.

Instead, the week’s moves point towards Eisenkot working with the ultra-Orthodox: right-wing anti-Netanyahu leader Avigdor Liberman, just approved as chair of the parliament’s Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee, suggested working with military leaders, the High Court and religious leaders to compromise on any ultra-Orthodox conscription bill, the Times of Israel reported.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

The body of a slain woman was discovered “lying in the leaves” near a popular trail just hours after she arrived at the scenic spot with her recently adopted dog — which was found unharmed days later.

A shocked bystander stumbled upon the body of Lizeht Rodriguez, 24, last Wednesday while walking on the trails between Northlake Nature Center and Pelican Park in St. Tammany Parish, according to the St. Tammany Parish Sheriff’s Office.

Rodriguez was found dead, “lying in the leaves,” roughly an hour and a half after arriving in the wooded area with her dog, Evie, in her silver Honda Civic around 12:30 p.m., according to cops and Nola.com.

Her death has since been ruled a homicide, though authorities have not yet released information about the cause of her death.

Rodriguez’s dog, Evie, whom she recently adopted, was located and picked up by a good Samaritan days after the tragedy, according to the St. Tammany Parish Department of Animal Services.

Evie suffered no physical injuries or wounds, and Rodriguez’s family has since claimed her, the department said.

A heartbreaking GoFundMe fundraiser started by Rodriguez’s sister for her burial and funeral costs described her as the “baby of the house.”

“Lizeht Rodriguez was only 24 years old and had her whole life ahead of her. She was the baby of the house, and losing someone so young is unbearable,” Nayma Rodriguez wrote in the fundraiser statement.

“The pain has affected every part of our daily lives. Right now, our family is struggling to work because of the extreme grief we are carrying.”

Investigators said they can’t yet rule out that a stranger killed Rodriguez on the popular trails, where there are no cameras.

“We cannot rule out the possibility of the murder being [done by] a stranger to Lizeht,” Interim Sheriff Bret Ibert said at a press conference on Friday, Nola.com reported.

Police have urged anyone near Pelican Park or the Northlake Nature Center last Wednesday between noon and 2 p.m. to contact investigators and review photos and dashcam footage — emphasizing that no detail is too small.

“Even if you believe you saw nothing unusual, we encourage you to think back to that afternoon. Did you notice anything that seemed out of place?” the St. Tammany Parish Sheriff’s Office wrote in a Facebook post.

“No detail is too small. Please do not assume someone else has already reported what you saw,” the department wrote.

“We ask the public to continue being vigilant, but not to spread fear or speculation,” the statement said. “Our priority remains finding answers for Lizeht’s family and bringing the person responsible to justice.”

Anyone with information is asked to contact the St. Tammany Parish Sheriff’s Office at 985-898-2338.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

LeBron James sat out the 76ers’ 135-123 victory in Brooklyn on Monday, one day after moving even higher on the NBA’s all-time assists list.

The 41-year-old James missed his fourth game of the season — all wins — due to management of a lower-back injury, sitting out the second night of back-to-back games.

The NBA’s all-time scoring leader passed former Nets point guard Jason Kidd for third on the all-time assists list in Sunday’s win over the Pacers.

The Sixers also posted wins over the Hornets, the Bucks and the Raptors in the previous games James missed during his first season in Philadelphia. He is averaging 15.1 points, 7.2 rebounds and 6.9 assists in his first 11 appearances.

Joel Embiid netted a season-best 37 points in his return to the Sixers lineup after sitting out their win over Indiana to manage a foot issue.

Nets forward Josh Minott was fined $25,000 by the NBA for making an obscene gesture late in Saturday’s game against the Grizzlies.

The 23-year-old Minott is averaging 3.4 points in 6.7 minutes per game, including just two minutes played in Sunday’s loss. The Nets signed the 6-8 forward to a two-year deal worth $9 million over the summer.

Nets leading scorer Michael Porter Jr. had 25 points in his return to the starting lineup for the Nets after he sat out Sunday’s loss in Memphis for personal reasons. He replaced Noah Clowney, who had played 35 minutes in his first start of the season against the Grizzlies.

Nolan Traore replaced Danny Wolf and tied his career high with 23 points on 7-for-12 shooting in 30 minutes.

Wolf had started the previous four games at shooting guard after receiving five DNP’s earlier in the season. He averaged 11.3 points as a starter since contributing 13 off the bench Nov. 4, in a win over Charlotte.

news.originalContent:
The ongoing Israeli assault continues to have disastrous consequences for the people of southern Lebanon.

Kfar Reman, Lebanon – It was the morning of September 7 when we arrived at the site of an Israeli attack in the village of Kfar Reman in southern Lebanon. Bulldozers were digging through the rubble of a home destroyed in an overnight air strike, searching for the bodies of two children.

Ten members of the same family, spanning three generations, had already been found in the building’s collapsed rooms, among them two survivors.

Two months later, I met 10-year-old Zainab and her eight-year-old brother Mustafa. After losing their parents and elder sister, Fatima, and their one-month-old brother, Ahmed, they now live with their grandmother. Both were thrown out of the house due to the intensity of the blast, but their physical wounds were no longer visible.

Zainab had a constant smile, but she was hiding sadness which she did not know how to express in words.

Mustafa was different. There was no smile. He is angry at Israel. When I asked him to share his story or a message to the world instead of speaking to me, he looked straight at the camera.

“What they did is they took my home and my parents from me,” Mustafa said. He paused for a few seconds and continued, “Because of them I no longer live in peace.”

More than a thousand children were injured in Israeli attacks between March and August this year, according to the United Nations.

Some lost a parent or both their parents while more than 260 were killed. That figure represents an average of seven children killed or injured every day over those six months – nearly double the number at the start of the latest on-again, off-again conflict between Hezbollah and Israel in late 2023.

We have repeatedly filmed children’s clothes, toys and school books among the rubble of homes destroyed in Israeli strikes, and repeatedly attended funerals of children killed alongside their parents. It is just as difficult emotionally to talk to survivors who show signs of trauma and tell us they live in fear.

In the village of Tibnine, close to the northern edge of the area occupied by the Israeli army, 11-year-old Bannine took us to the second floor of an orphanage, to show us what a nearby Israeli air strike did to their rooms.

“We were not here when this happened,” Bannine told us in a room full of debris and broken glass. Stuffed animals and clothes were still scattered on the floor.

Hundreds of thousands of people returned to their villages in southern Lebanon because of a reduction in violence in recent months. But there is little sense of security, with Israeli strikes and home demolitions continuing in front line areas.

“We wake up and sleep to the sound of bombing and warplanes and irritating drones,” Anaya Sultan told us. Her father was killed when the Israeli military escalated the conflict earlier this year. “He was my soul … he was everything to me,” she added.

Some of the girls here are not orphans, but their parents are too poor to care for them. According to Lebanese officials, the region’s economy is in a state of collapse.

Recurring conflicts, ruined infrastructure, blocked access to agricultural land, and mass displacement are making it hard for families in southern Lebanon to sustain themselves.

The UN identified southern Lebanon – alongside impoverished northern and eastern regions such as Akkar and Baalbek – as areas of greatest concern where families are struggling to survive.

According to a joint report released by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Food Programme (WFP), and Lebanon’s Ministry of Agriculture, more than 1 million people in Lebanon – about 21 percent of the recorded population – are facing crisis levels of acute food insecurity.

“Unfortunately, so many people are displaced … many of them used to support and help us. They are not present and they themselves are struggling,” Bassima Fawaz, who helps manage the orphanage, told us as we walked through the cold hallways and rooms of the building.

“We had to cover the windows with plastic sheeting because there’s no money to replace the glass shattered by Israeli bombardment. One of our girls is in hospital with pneumonia.”

Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Mollie Walker about the inside buzz on the Rangers.

Pavel Dorofeyev missed the game against the Canadiens on Monday with a lower-body injury despite head coach Mike Sullivan saying the past two days that he wasn’t concerned about Dorofeyev — who exited their practice Sunday for precautionary reasons — missing time. Sullivan said Monday morning that Dorofeyev participated in their optional morning skate.

Will Cuylle took Dorofeyev’s spot on the second line and scored a pair of goals, while Matt Rempe drew into the lineup for just the sixth time this season and skated on the fourth line. Eeli Tolvanen moved up to the third line, joining Noah Laba and Oliver Bjorkstrand.

When asked what went into ultimately keeping Dorofeyev out, Sullivan just said he was being evaluated for the injury.

In a season already filled with injuries, Dorofeyev’s added another one to their list. Their campaign was altered in the sixth game, when franchise goaltender Igor Shesterkin sustained a season-ending knee injury. Joe Veleno is on long-term injured reserve.

Alberts Smits and Sean Durzi are on injured reserve too. Joonas Korpisalo didn’t make his season debut until Nov. 7 — and didn’t make his MSG debut with the Blueshirts until Monday.

news.originalContent:
The Leonids, among the year’s fastest meteors, peak on November 17-18. Find the best time to watch in your city.

Some of the fastest meteors in the night sky return this week, as the Leonid meteor shower peaks on the night between November 17 and 18.

Racing at about 71km (44 miles) per second, they burn up as bright streaks, sometimes leaving glowing trails that hang in the sky for seconds.

In this visual explainer, see how the shower forms as Earth crosses a comet’s dust trail, then search for your city to find the best viewing time.

A meteor shower happens when dozens, or sometimes hundreds, of “shooting stars” streak across the night sky. In reality, they are not stars, but tiny bits of space debris burning up in Earth’s atmosphere.

Most of this debris comes from comets, which are icy bodies that orbit the sun and shed dust as they get closer to it. When Earth’s orbit crosses one of these dust trails, the particles, called meteoroids, hit the atmosphere at high speed and heat up. They glow as meteors and usually burn up long before reaching the ground.

The Leonids come from Comet Tempel-Tuttle, whose dust trail Earth passes through every November. Drag the slider below to follow Earth through 2026 and see when it meets the stream.

The Leonids are named after the constellation Leo, the point in the sky from which they appear to come. They are known for fireballs, which are unusually bright meteors from larger bits of debris. They also produce Earth-grazers, meteors that skim the upper atmosphere at a shallow angle and leave long trails near the horizon.

What really sets them apart is their storms. Comet Tempel-Tuttle passes close to the sun about every 33 years and leaves debris behind. When that happens, the shower can produce a storm of at least 1,000 meteors an hour.

The 1833 storm over North America helped scientists work out where meteors come from. In 1966, thousands of meteors fell every minute for about 15 minutes. The most recent storms came in 1999, 2001 and 2002, and the comet next swings close to the sun in 2031.

The Leonids can appear in any part of the sky, so the best approach is to find a dark spot with a wide view, lie back and take in as much sky as you can.

If you trace their paths backwards, the meteors all seem to streak out from a single point known as the radiant. This is an effect of perspective: the debris travels along roughly parallel paths, but the meteors appear to spread out from one point, much like railway tracks seem to meet in the distance.

For the Leonids, the radiant lies in the constellation Leo, which rises in the east around midnight.

According to the International Meteor Organization (IMO), the Leonids are active from November 6 to 30 and are expected to peak on the night between November 17 and 18, around 23:45 GMT on Tuesday. Under clear, dark skies, the IMO expects up to about 15 meteors an hour at the peak.

The best time to watch is between midnight and dawn, as Leo climbs higher in the sky. The moon, which will be about half full on the peak night, sets around midnight in many places, leaving darker skies for the rest of the night.

Find a spot away from city lights and give your eyes about 20 minutes to adjust to the dark.

Use the widget below to find the best viewing times in your city.

Yes. The Leonids are visible from the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere, but conditions are generally better in the north, where Leo climbs higher in the sky. South of the equator, the best chance is in the hour or two before dawn.

Only slightly. The moon reaches its first quarter on November 17 and sets around midnight, so it should not interfere much during the best viewing hours.

The Leonids are far from the busiest shower. Under ideal conditions, the IMO puts their peak rate at about 15 meteors an hour, compared with about 100 for the Perseids in August and about 150 for the Geminids in December. What they lack in numbers, they make up for in speed and their history of storms.

news.originalContent:
(Photo by Leon Neal/Getty Images)

Britain has opened an investigation into Russell Brand for telling supporters from prison that he is innocent.

Downing Street called the message appalling and said it is being urgently investigated, the BBC reported. The government expects action if the comedian broke prison rules. His wife, Laura, read the statement on the couple’s Sunday Service show on YouTube, the BBC stated.

“As you know, I am not guilty for the offenses I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening,” Brand said in the message. (RELATED: Russell Brand’s Wife Breaks Silence By Reading His Jailhouse Message)

Prison rules bar inmates from making statements that distress victims, the prime minister’s spokesman told the BBC. Media contact is allowed only in rare cases. “Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments,” the spokesman said.

The restriction predates Brand. Guidance from 2010 lets inmates reach the media by letter, phone or visit only in exceptional cases, according to the Ministry of Justice instruction PSI 37/2010. It sits under Prison Rules 34 and 35 across England and Wales.

Labour Justice Secretary Alex Norris called the broadcast “completely unacceptable,” the BBC reported. He said on X that he expects action if Brand broke the rules.

The broadcast of a statement from Russell Brand is completely unacceptable. Prisoners are rightly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims. This is being urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules.

Prison governors can cut social visits or strip privileges such as gym time and television, the BBC stated. They can also block phone numbers or increase call monitoring.

The innocence claims will “certainly retraumatise his victims and other survivors of rape who have to hear it,” Andrea Simon, the victims’ commissioner for London, told BBC Radio 4.

A jury convicted Brand of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women. A judge sentenced him Nov. 9 to 10 years and six months. A jury acquitted him of two other rape counts and one attempted indecent assault, according to the Daily Wire. Officials moved him from HMP Wandsworth to HMP Littlehey, a prison that mainly holds sex offenders, the BBC reported.
